sentences.text: This giant dinosaur measured between 21 and 23 meters in length and weighed from 16.4 to 22.4 tonnes.
It belonged to the diplodocid family, a group of sauropod dinosaurs known for their long necks and tails.
Unlike its relative Diplodocus, Apatosaurus possessed shorter neck vertebrae that were built more heavily.
Its bones contained internal air sacs that created a porous structure to help reduce overall body weight.
The genus was first named and described by Othniel Charles Marsh in the year 1877.
The species designated as the type for this genus is Apatosaurus ajax.
A second species, Apatosaurus louisae, was later identified by Holland in 1916.
Marsh originally named many species based on small, fragmentary remains that were difficult to distinguish from one another.
As a generalist herbivore, it likely held its head at an elevated position while feeding.
Researchers believe the tail might have functioned like a whip to generate loud sounds for communication.
Brontosaurus is the sole other genus within the subfamily Apatosaurinae, while other genera are now seen as synonyms or reclassified diplodocines.
Most modern experts agree that Apatosaurus and Brontosaurus should be treated as a single genus.
Marsh originally separated Apatosaurus from Atlantosaurus by counting sacral vertebrae, claiming the former had three and the latter had four.
However, recent studies suggest these distinguishing traits were widespread, making many such separate taxa invalid.
These animals lived approximately 152 to 151 million years ago during the Late Jurassic period.
Fossil evidence has been recovered from the Morrison Formation in states including Colorado, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Wyoming, and Utah.
Specimens belonging to Apatosaurus ajax specifically date to the late Kimmeridgian through the early Tithonian ages.
All known remains of Apatosaurus louisae come from the late Kimmeridgian layers at Dinosaur National Monument.
Scientists continue to debate whether Brontosaurus represents a distinct genus from Apatosaurus, as a 2015 study supports the separation but consensus is not universal.
Some researchers propose Apatosaurus may have possessed a skull similar to Camarasaurus, based on a disarticulated tooth found at an Apatosaurus site.
Although scientifically invalid, the name Brontosaurus remains popular due to a famous mount created by the American Museum of Natural History.
The skulls used for the museum's Apatosaurus display were likely borrowed from Camarasaurus, the only sauropod with known skull material available at that time.
Elmer Riggs concluded that the differences between Apatosaurus and Brontosaurus were invalid because the holotype of Apatosaurus ajax was an immature specimen.
